content: The action plan emphasizes the importance of tailoring oral health interventions to the specific context of each country, taking into account available resources and capacities. It provides detailed guidance on service components and interventions to address the most prevalent oral diseases, as well as the core elements required for a national oral health program. Monitoring the implementation and tracking progress are integral aspects of the plan, which aligns with the Global Oral Health Action Plan (2023–2030) and its associated monitoring framework, set to be adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2023. National governments, health ministries, and a broad range of stakeholders—including subnational administrations, health regulatory bodies, professional associations, educational institutions, research entities, civil society organizations, media, development partners, individuals, families, and communities—play critical roles in promoting oral health and ensuring actionable outcomes. Their responsibilities span leadership, management, support, financing, advocacy, communication, and the promotion of oral health to improve overall oral health status. Specific roles and responsibilities for key stakeholders in implementing the South-East Asia Regional Oral Health Action Plan (2022–2030) are outlined in Section 5 of the document. The WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia, along with its country offices, will provide leadership and coordination to promote and monitor the implementation of the action plan. WHO will also offer technical support in collaboration with WHO collaborating centers and other partners to strengthen national responses to the oral disease burden. Additional technical documents and guidance will be developed to support national implementation, aligned with the forthcoming Global Oral Health Action Plan (2023–2030) and related guidance. WHO will further facilitate knowledge exchange among Member States to advance progress toward universal health coverage for oral health by 2030. Oral health is recognized as a critical component of public health, given its significant impact on overall health and its interrelation with noncommunicable diseases (NCDs). In May 2021, the World Health Assembly adopted Resolution WHA74/A74/R5 on oral health, requesting the development of a global strategy to address oral diseases. This strategy, adopted in May 2022, aims to integrate oral health into universal health coverage (UHC) by 2030. It focuses on six strategic objectives: oral health governance, promotion and prevention, workforce development, integration into primary health care (PHC) and UHC, information systems, and research. The Global Oral Health Action Plan (2023–2030) complements this strategy, incorporating evidence-based interventions with proven cost-effectiveness. It also addresses the prevention and control of NCDs, including oral health, and emphasizes the need for measurable targets and a monitoring framework. The plan is designed to support Member States in translating strategic guidance into impactful national actions. Oral health encompasses the state of the mouth, teeth, and orofacial structures, enabling essential functions such as eating, breathing, and speaking. It also includes psychosocial dimensions like self-confidence, well-being, and the ability to socialize and work without pain or embarrassment. Poor oral health has profound social, economic, and psychological consequences, negatively affecting quality of life. It varies across the life course and is integral to general health, supporting individuals in achieving their potential and participating in society. The burden of oral diseases in the South-East Asia Region is significant, with high prevalence and strong inequalities. Vulnerable and disadvantaged populations face higher disease burdens and limited access to prevention, care, and rehabilitation services. In 2019, the region reported over 900 million cases of untreated dental caries, severe periodontal diseases, and edentulism. Other conditions, such as orofacial clefts, dental trauma, and oral manifestations of systemic diseases, further contribute to the burden. The region also faces a shortage of dental personnel and geographic disparities in their distribution. Oral health care is often associated with high out-of-pocket expenditures, leading to catastrophic financial impacts for poorer households. The Strategy for Oral Health in South-East Asia (2013–2020) aimed to achieve the highest attainable oral health status for all people in the region, enabling them to lead healthy and productive lives. It set two overarching targets: a 25% reduction in premature mortality from oral cancer and a 25% reduction in the prevalence of dental caries by 2025. The strategy focused on advocacy, integration into UHC, community involvement, promotion and prevention, and oral health systems development. Priority areas included integrating oral health with NCDs, addressing oral cancer, promoting fluoride use, diversifying the oral health workforce, and strengthening school oral health programs. A review of the strategy's implementation revealed progress in some areas but persistent challenges in others. For example, eight Member States had dedicated oral health policies, and five had conducted national oral health surveys. However, significant gaps remain in workforce integration, fluoride regulation, and mercury phase-out policies. The findings highlight the need for continued efforts to address oral health challenges and reduce inequalities across the region. The Action Plan for Oral Health in South-East Asia (2022–2030) builds on the previous strategy and aligns with the Global Oral Health Strategy. It identifies six strategic action areas, each with core actions relevant to all countries and additional optional actions based on national priorities and resources. The plan aims to accelerate national responses to achieve agreed targets and promote universal oral health coverage by 2030. Its vision is to empower all people in the region to enjoy the highest attainable oral health status, enabling them to lead healthy and productive lives.
